name: Eighth Amendment
kicker: No excessive bail or fines, no cruel and unusual punishments · Ratified 1791
briefing: The Eighth Amendment is one of the shortest parts of the Bill of Rights, just sixteen words long: “Excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted.” Its wording comes almost straight from England’s Bill of Rights of 1689. Supreme Court cases about the death penalty, prison conditions, and sentences for teenagers have all turned on what “cruel and unusual” means.
answerHtml: Eighth Amendment (or Amendment VIII; prompt on cruel and unusual punishment, excessive bail, or excessive fines; do not accept “Bill of Rights” or other amendment numbers)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In _Trop v. Dulles_, Earl Warren wrote that this amendment “must draw its meaning from the evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society.” That 1958 case held that a wartime deserter could not be stripped of his citizenship as punishment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this part of the Bill of Rights that bans excessive bail, excessive fines, and “cruel and unusual punishments.”

tossups.p: In _Stack v. Boyle_, a 1951 case involving Communist Party members charged under the Smith Act, the Supreme Court ruled under this amendment that bail set higher than needed to make sure a defendant returns for trial is too high.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, part of the Bill of Rights, that bans excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In a 2019 case, Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote for a unanimous Supreme Court that one clause of this amendment applies to the states, after Indiana tried to take away Tyson Timbs’s $42,000 Land Rover, worth more than four times the largest fine allowed for his crime.
tossups.r: That clause bans excessive fines. For 10 points, name this amendment that also outlaws cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In one 1972 case decided under this amendment, all nine justices wrote separate opinions, and Thurgood Marshall and William Brennan argued that the death penalty is always unconstitutional. The 5–4 decision itself was a short unsigned opinion.
tossups.r: That case, _Furman v. Georgia_, struck down the death penalty laws then in use. For 10 points, name this amendment banning cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In _Weems v. United States_, a 1910 case from the Philippines, the Supreme Court read the words also found in this amendment to mean that punishments must be in proportion to the crime. The case involved a harsh sentence for an official who had falsified government records.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, ratified in 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights, that bans cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In _Robinson v. California_ (1962), the Supreme Court first used the Fourteenth Amendment to apply part of this amendment to the states, striking down a state law that punished a person for having an illness rather than for any act.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that forbids excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: George Mason put almost the same words as this amendment into the Virginia Declaration of Rights in 1776. At Virginia’s ratifying convention, Patrick Henry complained that the proposed Constitution had no such protection.
tossups.r: Its wording came from England’s Bill of Rights of 1689. For 10 points, name this amendment that bans cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In a 2005 opinion, Anthony Kennedy pointed to “the overwhelming weight of international opinion” while ruling that this amendment bars the death penalty for crimes committed before age 18. That 5–4 decision overruled _Stanford v. Kentucky_, a 1989 case.
tossups.r: That case was _Roper v. Simmons_. For 10 points, name this amendment that bans cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In _Atkins v. Virginia_ (2002), the Supreme Court ruled that this amendment bars the death penalty for people with intellectual disabilities, noting that a growing number of states had already banned the practice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, part of the Bill of Rights, that outlaws cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In _Graham v. Florida_ and _Miller v. Alabama_, the Supreme Court used this amendment to limit sentences of life in prison without parole for people who committed crimes as teenagers, pointing out that young people have a greater ability to change.
tossups.r: Those 2010 and 2012 cases built on _Roper v. Simmons_. For 10 points, name this amendment banning cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In _Estelle v. Gamble_ (1976), the Supreme Court ruled that prison officials who show “deliberate indifference” to an inmate’s serious medical needs violate this amendment. The case was brought by a Texas prisoner who hurt his back while doing prison work.
tossups.r: That same year, _Gregg v. Georgia_ allowed states to use new death penalty laws. For 10 points, name this amendment banning cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In _Brown v. Plata_ (2011), Anthony Kennedy wrote for a 5–4 majority that crowding in California’s prisons had made medical care so poor that it violated this amendment, and he upheld an order to reduce the prison population.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, part of the Bill of Rights, that bans cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In _Ewing v. California_ (2003), the Supreme Court ruled that a “three strikes” sentence of 25 years to life for a man with earlier serious convictions who had stolen three golf clubs did not violate this amendment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that bans excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: This amendment is only sixteen words long, and its wording comes almost exactly from England’s Bill of Rights of 1689, passed after the Glorious Revolution put William and Mary on the throne.
tossups.r: Its first clause forbids excessive bail. For 10 points, name this amendment that also bans cruel and unusual punishments.

tossups.p: In _United States v. Salerno_ (1987), the Supreme Court ruled that the Bail Reform Act of 1984, which lets judges hold some dangerous defendants in jail before trial without bail, did not violate this amendment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment whose first clause bans excessive bail and whose last clause bans cruel and unusual punishments.

trap.title: Amendment, clause, or case?
trap.body: This amendment is one part of the Bill of Rights, so “Bill of Rights” is wrong when a question asks for one amendment. Its neighbors are easy to mix up: the Fifth protects against self-incrimination and double jeopardy, and the Sixth guarantees a speedy trial and a lawyer. Saying only “cruel and unusual punishment” or “excessive bail” earns a prompt, and the Eighteenth Amendment (Prohibition) is a different number entirely.
trap.fix: Bail, fines, “cruel and unusual,” “evolving standards of decency,” the death penalty, and cases like _Furman_, _Gregg_, _Roper_, and _Timbs_ all mean the Eighth Amendment. If the question asks for “this clause,” name the specific clause; if it asks for “this amendment,” say “Eighth Amendment.”
